sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Pinal County
sections.html:
Take a deed to the Pinal County Recorder's Office. Florence has the main office, and four others spread across the county. An instrument is recorded in Pinal County when the property sits in the county (A.R.S. 11-468). The same office also handles voter registration and early voting.

Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132. Don't expect a notary there. Staff also may not advise you on legal matters, help complete a form or pick a document type for you. Bring those questions to a title company, escrow officer or attorney.

Arizona law requires the grantor to sign the deed and acknowledge the signature before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). Get the deed notarized first, then send it on.

Pinal County covers 5,374 square miles, so the Recorder runs five offices. Each is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Pinal County?
sections.html:
The standard fee is $30 per document, and it falls to $15 when the United States, the state or a political subdivision asks for the recording. The Recording Fee Schedule took effect July 1, 2019 and follows the amendment to A.R.S. 11-475(A). The $30 already covers the affidavit of property value, extra indexing and the document and storage fee surcharge, and each recording fee includes $1 for postage to mail the document back.

  • Subdivision plats or maps (24 by 36 inches): $24, plus $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Survey and other maps (18 by 24 inches): $24, plus $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Plats and survey maps recorded at a government agency's request: $14 for the first sheet and $10 for each additional sheet.
  • Copies of recorded documents: $1 per page, with return postage included on mail requests, plus $3 per document for certification.

All of these are flat amounts. Nothing scales with the price of your house. Your title company can confirm that no other charge applies at closing.

You can record in person at any of the five offices, send the original by mail, or use one of the trusted e-recording partners the county works with. For mail, enclose a check or money order for the amount on the fee schedule. For e-recording, call an office and ask for the partner list. The online document search reaches back to May 23, 1980, and any image you download is stamped as an unofficial copy.

In-person filers need photo ID under A.R.S. 11-472. Exceptions cover documents submitted by an escrow office, a title insurer or agent, a bank or credit union, an active State Bar of Arizona member, or a government entity. When escrow handles your closing, the escrow office files the deed and you skip the ID rule.

After a compliant document comes in, staff process it in four stages.

  • If the form is complete and the fees are paid, it becomes a permanent public record.
  • Data entry builds an index so the record can be found by name.
  • The document is optically scanned and microfilmed to meet state archival requirements.
  • The original goes back to the address typed on it.

Layout rules for the paper itself are in A.R.S. 11-480. Expect a caption, original signatures, pages no bigger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches, type of ten point or larger, and a blank two inch strip at the top of page one.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and the affidavit of property value
sections.html:
The fee schedule has no charge tied to the sale price, so there is no separate transfer tax to budget for. What the buyer and seller do owe the Recorder is an Affidavit of Real Property Value. A.R.S. 11-1133 and 11-1137(B) require both sides, or their agents, to complete and attest to it, and skipping it is a class 2 misdemeanor. County assessors and the Department of Revenue use the data to build tables for uniform valuation. One sale does not directly change the assessment or taxes on that property.

Sign and notarize the affidavit, then hand it in with the deed. Exempt transfers skip it. The exempt list in A.R.S. 11-1134 covers gifts, quitclaims given for no money, trustee's deeds, and transfers made for only nominal consideration between spouses, between parent and child, between grandparent and grandchild, between siblings, or under a beneficiary deed.

For an exempt transfer, write the statute number and exemption code on the face of the deed beneath the legal description, for example "A.R.S. 11-1134 B3." Don't complete the affidavit in that case.

sections.h2: Fixing or removing something on a recorded record
sections.html:
Nothing on the public record can be edited in place. A recorded transfer stands until a later recorded document changes it. The Recorder can't advise on how to hold title or how to take a decedent's name off a deed, so take those questions to a title company or an attorney.

  • To find easements on your property, read Schedule B of your title policy if the purchase closed through a title company. Otherwise search the Recorder's website using one party's name and an approximate recording date.
  • To have personal information removed from public records, read the Arizona statutes for the Recorder (A.R.S. 11-483), the Assessor and Treasurer (A.R.S. 11-484) and voter registration (A.R.S. 16-153).

Suspicious filings can be referred to the FBI or other law enforcement. Presenting a false instrument for recording is a class 6 felony under A.R.S. 39-161.

sections.h2: Recording steps in a typical Pinal County sale
sections.html:
Few sellers ever stand at the recording counter. Here is how a normal sale reaches the Recorder.

  • You sign the deed before a notary, and you and the buyer sign the Affidavit of Real Property Value unless the transfer is exempt.
  • The title or escrow company checks the caption, signatures and margins against A.R.S. 11-480.
  • That company delivers the package to the Recorder, pays the fee and receives the recorded original back.
  • You ask the title company for a copy of the recorded deed, which is your proof of the transfer date.

If you sell for cash without a lender, the sequence is the same but shorter, because there is no loan document to record alongside the deed.

The county counts 539,380 residents, up from 425,264 in 2020. Owner-occupied homes make up 81.7 percent of housing, and the median owner-occupied value is $349,000 for 2020 to 2024. With that much growth, the Recorder's offices handle a steady flow of transfers.

faqs.q: How much does Pinal County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: $30 per document, or $15 for recordings requested by government bodies. The fee includes the affidavit of property value, indexing and the storage surcharge, plus $1 for mailing the document back. Plats and survey maps run $24 for the first sheet.

faqs.q: Where is the Pinal County Recorder's main office?
faqs.a: 31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence, AZ 85132. Branch offices operate in Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley. All are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed in Pinal County by mail or online?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original with a check or money order, or record electronically through a trusted e-recording partner. Call any Recorder office for the partner list.

faqs.q: Do I need to file an affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: Yes, unless the transfer is exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134. Buyers and sellers must complete it, and skipping it is a class 2 misdemeanor. For an exempt transfer, write the statute and exemption code on the face of the deed instead.

faqs.q: Can the Pinal County Recorder prepare my deed or notarize it?
faqs.a: No. The office offers no notary service and can't give legal advice or help with documents. Have an attorney, title company or escrow officer prepare the deed and arrange the notary.
